Getting started with knittogether

This article follows one report from the first Word draft to the finished output. It explains each step, then shows how to go back and forth with a colleague who edits in Word.

Three terms

Placeholder. Plain text in the Word document that marks where R output should go, such as placeholder_plot. It has two parts: a prefix that every placeholder shares (placeholder_) and an ID that says which piece of content goes there (plot). The prefix is up to you. Set it with placeholder_prefix, and it’s used exactly as you give it, so "xyz_" gives xyz_plot. Pick one that won’t turn up by accident in normal writing, and use the same one throughout. The same placeholder can appear more than once if you need the same output in several places.

Marker. When knittogether fills a placeholder, it leaves a small styled tag with the placeholder’s name next to the output. That’s how it finds the output again next time. You control markers with marker_mode.

Draft block. While the report is still a draft, each piece of R output is wrapped between DRAFT_CONTENT_START and DRAFT_CONTENT_END. The writer edits around these lines. When you bring the document back in, knittogether swaps each block for its placeholder so it can be filled again with fresh output.

The first pass

Suppose a colleague sends you draft.docx. They’ve typed placeholder_plot where a chart should go and placeholder_total where a count of rows should go.

library(knittogether)

1. Convert

convert_markdown() turns the Word file into Markdown. It keeps the headings, lists, tables, footnotes and citations, and saves the images into a media/ folder.

convert_markdown(
  input_file = "draft.docx",
  markdown_file = "draft.md",
  media_base_dir = "."
)

PowerPoint files work the same way. See vignette("powerpoint") for the differences.

2. Clean

clean_markdown() fixes things that Word leaves behind and Quarto doesn’t like.

clean_markdown(
  markdown_file = "draft.md",
  placeholder_prefix = "placeholder_",
  heading_offset = TRUE,
  clean_citations = TRUE
)

Here heading_offset = TRUE moves every heading down a level, because a Word “Heading 1” would otherwise become the page title in HTML. clean_citations = TRUE removes stray backslashes from citations. Pass your placeholder_prefix so knittogether can tidy up any Word formatting stuck to the placeholders.

3. Say what goes in each placeholder

define_content() describes one piece of content. placeholder_map() collects them all together.

plot <- define_content(
  placeholder_id = "plot",
  description = "Car weight against fuel economy",
  output_mode = "chunk",
  content = { plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg) },
  chunk_options = list(echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6)
)

total <- define_content(
  placeholder_id = "total",
  description = "Number of cars",
  output_mode = "inline",
  content = { nrow(mtcars) }
)

content <- placeholder_map(specs = list(plot, total))

output_mode decides how the content goes in:

  • "inline" puts a value inside a sentence, as inline R code.
  • "chunk" puts a code chunk on its own line, for plots, tables or anything longer.
  • "asis" pastes in text exactly as you give it.

The code in content isn’t run yet. It’s written into the Markdown and runs when Quarto renders the document.

description is optional but worth adding. It goes into the validation log (see step 4), which makes it much easier to check the right output has landed in the right place.

For a plain value that doesn’t need a description, you can skip define_content() and pass it straight to the map:

content <- placeholder_map(specs = list(plot), scalars = list(total = 32))

For longer pieces of analysis, put the code in a separate Quarto file and include it, for example content = "{{< include child_plot.qmd >}}". A few things help this go smoothly:

  • Keep the main .qmd, the child files and the Markdown in the same folder, so relative paths work when you render.
  • Leave the YAML header out of child files, so settings such as format don’t clash with the main document.
  • Make sure any data the child file uses has been loaded before it runs.

4. Fill the placeholders 

replace_placeholders(
  markdown_file = "draft.md",
  placeholder_prefix = "placeholder_",
  code_content = content,
  validation_path = "validation"
)

Each placeholder is swapped for its content. With validation_path set, knittogether also writes a log of which placeholders it found and filled, and what changed since the last run. If the quarto and reactable packages are installed you also get an HTML page that’s easier to browse. Smaller, more specific placeholders give you a more useful log.

To check that every image and table has alt text or a caption, pass the Markdown to accessibility_scan():

accessibility_scan(readLines("draft.md"))

5. Render

Include the Markdown in a Quarto document and render it:

---
title: "My report"
format: docx
---

{{< include draft.md >}}

Rendering to Word gives your colleague a draft with the R output in place. You can render the same file to HTML, PDF or PowerPoint by changing format.

replace_placeholders() also returns the Markdown invisibly, so you can insert it into a Quarto document directly instead of using an include.

Quarto can’t include a file that doesn’t exist yet, so the Markdown has to be built before each render. In a Quarto project you can make this happen automatically. Put the steps above in a script, say build.R, and add this to _quarto.yml:

project:
  pre-render: Rscript build.R

Going back and forth with Word

By default, replace_placeholders() runs with draft_mode = TRUE and marker_mode = "hidden". That’s what makes the round trip work: each piece of output sits in a draft block with a marker naming its placeholder.

When your colleague has edited the Word draft and sent it back:

  1. Convert the new version. If they save new copies into a folder, latest_word_file("drafts") finds the most recent one.

  2. Clean it with clear_draft = TRUE. This turns each draft block back into its placeholder. Use the same placeholder_prefix you filled the draft with. If you don’t, the placeholders won’t be recognised and the draft content is removed with nothing to refill it.

    clean_markdown(
  markdown_file = "draft.md",
  placeholder_prefix = "placeholder_",
  clear_draft = TRUE
)

  3. Fill the placeholders again with replace_placeholders(). Your output is refreshed, not duplicated, so you can update the analysis at the same time.

Ask your colleague to leave the DRAFT_CONTENT_START and DRAFT_CONTENT_END lines alone. Everything around them is theirs to edit. If those lines get in the way, you can set up a Word style that hides them until you press ¶. vignette("office-styling") shows how, and the package includes an example document already set up this way:

system.file("extdata", "PlaceholderMarker_example.docx", package = "knittogether")

The final version

When the words are final, fill the placeholders one last time with draft mode and markers turned off:

replace_placeholders(
  markdown_file = "draft.md",
  placeholder_prefix = "placeholder_",
  code_content = content,
  draft_mode = FALSE,
  marker_mode = "off"
)

You can run this straight on the latest draft: any draft blocks are removed first. The result has no placeholder names or markers left in it.

Only do this at the end. With marker_mode = "off" there’s nothing left to show where the output came from, so a document rendered this way can’t be brought back in and refreshed.

Keeping earlier versions

By default each step overwrites its file. To keep a history instead, give clean_markdown() or replace_placeholders() an output_file, and use timestamped_path() to add the date and time to the name:

replace_placeholders(
  markdown_file = "draft.md",
  placeholder_prefix = "placeholder_",
  code_content = content,
  output_file = timestamped_path("drafts/draft.md")
)

Set overwrite = FALSE if you’d rather get an error than overwrite an existing file.

Running every step at once

run_workflow() runs convert, clean and replace in one call. Give it any argument the three functions take. Each step uses the previous step’s output. If you give a folder as input_file, it uses the newest Word or PowerPoint file in it, and base_name narrows the choice to files whose names start with that text.

run_workflow(
  input_file = "drafts",
  base_name = "report",
  markdown_file = "report.md",
  placeholder_prefix = "placeholder_",
  heading_offset = TRUE,
  code_content = content
)
